question: The Parliament recently adopted a resolution entitled ‘My voice, my choice’. Although the Union must respect the sovereignty of Member States in matters of health, this text pushes for legislative standardisation with federalist overtones. In the text, the legislature seriously overlooks the protection of healthcare professionals and subsidiarity in favour of the Member States in this area.

By describing the right to refuse as an ‘obstacle’, the resolution undermines the conscience clause, which not only constitutes a pillar of employment law and individual freedom, but was also once an objection recognised for those working in the military. The Commission cannot, under the guise of financial mechanisms, compel healthcare professionals to act against their ethical convictions.
This aberration ignores the fact that individual freedom ends where respect for local laws and the conscience of others begins. 1.
How does the Commission intend to protect the right of refusal of healthcare professionals as a legal right, when the resolution describes this as an ‘obstacle’ that needs to be removed?
What guarantees will the Commission provide to ensure that workers do not suffer from discrimination in the workplace in the name of a European financial solidarity mechanism?
How does it intend to prevent this financial support from acting as a federalist lever for interfering in the national organisation of health services?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Marcin Sypniewski (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.2026) The obligation to ensure a high level of human health protection when drawing up and implementing all EU policies and activities is enshrined in Articles 9 and 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.

Article 168(7) of the Treaty provides that EU action shall respect the responsibilities of the Member States for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care.

In line with the Treaties, the Commission’s reply to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’1, does not create obligations for any Member State or healthcare practitioner to provide abortion services, in full respect of the Member States competence in this area.
It is for the Member States, not for the EU, to regulate the right of healthcare providers to object to provide certain healthcare services on grounds of ethical convictions.
